options: Reads a CSV file directly into a DataFrame, using the header row as column names
Converts a DataFrame back into a CSV file
Only works for files already inside Power BI
Requires manually specifying every column name and type first
questions.explain: pd.read_csv() is the standard way to load a file into a DataFrame — it reads the header row as column names and infers each column's data type automatically.

questions.q: What three checks does the lesson recommend before trusting a freshly loaded CSV?
options: .shape, .dtypes, and .head() to check row/column counts, types, and a preview of the actual data
Only checking the file size on disk
Printing every single row before doing anything else
Renaming every column before checking anything
questions.explain: Checking shape (row/column counts), dtypes (are types what you expected), and head() (a quick visual sanity check) catches problems before they propagate into later work.

questions.q: Where in Power BI Desktop do you run a Python script as a data source?
options: Home ribbon → Get Data → Other → Python script
File → Options → Python scripting
Insert → Python Visual
It can only be done outside Power BI, never inside it
questions.explain: Get Data, then Other, then Python script is the exact path — the same category R script sits in, run from the Home ribbon.

questions.q: Does the script you tested on your own machine need to be rewritten to work inside Power BI's Python script dialog?
options: No — the exact same script, including the import pandas as pd line, is pasted in as-is
Yes, every variable name must be changed to match Power BI's naming rules
Yes, the import statement must be removed before pasting
Power BI only accepts scripts written in a special Power BI-specific syntax
questions.explain: The exact code already tested locally gets pasted directly into the Script field — nothing about it needs to be rewritten for Power BI specifically.

questions.q: What does the Navigator window show after a Python script runs successfully in Power BI?
options: Every DataFrame the script created, ready to select and load into the model
A list of every Python library installed on the machine
The script's raw text for editing
A live preview of Matplotlib charts only
questions.explain: The Navigator lists the DataFrames produced by the script (commonly named after the variable, like 'df') so you can select and load one into your Power BI model.
